Ronald Acuña Jr. continues to be one of the hottest hitters in baseball this September, hitting .342 with an OPS approaching 1.100. That late-season run got even more impressive over the weekend, when he locked up a 20/20 season despite missing more than 50 games to injury — the third time in his career he's cleared 20 home runs in a season shortened by at least 50 missed games.
Acuña hasn't just been one of the best hitters in baseball this month; he's reminded everyone he's one of the sport's biggest draws whenever he's healthy. Which raises the obvious question: Will the Atlanta Braves sign their franchise slugger long-term?
There are a few layers to that. Acuña is in the final guaranteed year of an eight-year, $100 million extension, with two club options for 2027 and 2028 that the Braves will undoubtedly exercise. But according to multiple analysts, a long-term deal getting done before he reaches free agency is far from certain, given both his injury history and general manager Alex Anthopoulos's general reluctance to make massive long-term commitments.
That hesitation has precedent. Anthopoulos and the Braves have let franchise cornerstones like Freddie Freeman, Dansby Swanson and Max Fried all walk away in recent offseasons, betting he could find comparable production for less money elsewhere — and largely, that bet has paid off, even if the solutions haven't all come from the same place.
Matt Olson, acquired via trade, has effectively replaced Freeman's production at first base, and a wave of young, club-controlled arms developed within Atlanta's own system has kept the rotation competitive behind Chris Sale even as Fried starred elsewhere.
Shortstop is a bit different. Mauricio Dubón has helped the Braves finally find a viable shortstop, whch they had been looking for since Swanson's departure. But even he's more of a stopgap in 2026 than the long-term answer, with genuine farm system options like Tatie Southisene, John Gil and Alex Lodise all competing to be the shortstop of the future.
Say what you want about those moves, but collectively, they worked. Freeman, Fried and Swanson are all great, even star-caliber players. Freeman is a future Hall of Famer. Yet, Atlanta found a way to replace each of them anyway.
Acuña is a different animal entirely. He's not just a star; he's a superstar, a sparkplug, the conduit every other piece of this offense runs through. We've already seen how much the Braves struggle with outfield-by-committee whenever he or Michael Harris II has to miss time.
Compare that to shortstop, where prospects like Southisene, Gil and Lodise are all competing to be the long-term answer, or even the rotation, where the system has produced options — the outfield simply doesn't have that same kind of depth waiting in the wings anymore. That makes keeping Acuña in Atlanta feel less like a preference and more like a necessity.
Acuña has an MVP under his belt, which he won after an unprecedented 40/70 season. Sure, they've let an MVP walk before, Freeman, an replaced him with an All-Star in Olson. Good luck doing that again and with even better ballplayer like Acuña.
That's why Acuña could be an exception to Anthopoulos's usual approach, and why he'll ultimately open up the checkbook before Acuña reaches unrestricted free agency in 2029.
There's also the competitive angle to consider. If Anthopoulos were to let Acuña walk, which teams are aggressive enough spenders to actually land him? The Mets, Phillies and Dodgers top that list — and even with Anthopoulos's track record of letting players leave for greener pastures, it's hard to imagine him handing one of the game's most electric superstars to one of Atlanta's three most bitter rivals.
The Braves face plenty of tough contract questions, but this one might be the most straightforward. Time will tell, but I think Anthopoulos will ultimately make the right call.

The Atlanta Braves and Boston Red Sox are both preparing for postseason pushes, but their paths since one of the most consequential recent trades between the clubs could hardly look more different.
Boston traded likely Hall of Famer Chris Sale to Atlanta before the 2024 season, receiving Vaughn Grissom in return while also sending $17 million to the Braves. At the time, Sale was coming off several injury-plagued seasons, having made just 31 starts from 2020 through 2023. The Red Sox appeared to be moving on from an accomplished pitcher whose best days might have been behind him.
Instead, Sale has experienced a remarkable career revival in Atlanta, leaving many Red Sox fans embittered by the decision to part ways with him.
"Sale entered the 2024 season thinking it would be the last of his career, and he exited it with his first career Cy Young Award," Mark Bowman wrote for MLB.com. "Injuries had limited him to 151 innings from 2021-23. But he has continued to get better through each of his first three seasons with Atlanta."
Now, with both teams looking toward October, Sale has offered a revealing response about that fateful transaction.
Atlanta Braves' Chris Sale Offers 3-Word Response On Boston Red Sox Trade
During a recent interview with Baseball Is Dead, Sale was asked whether he believed he would have enjoyed the same career renaissance if he had remained with the Red Sox.
"I don't know," Sale responded several tines. "I get traded and I found a new trainer… And I really felt like that helped me a lot with my health."
While Red Sox fans will never know if Sale would have been able to deliver a similar 2024 campaign in Boston, the Braves' superstar did go on to suggest he was only able to maintain his health thanks to a new training program away from Red Sox facilities.
Atlanta Braves' Star Chris Sale Sends Message On Health Issues With Boston Red Sox
The results since the trade have been striking. Sale posted an 18-3 record with a 2.38 ERA and 225 strikeouts in 2024, winning his first Cy Young Award at age 35.
His comments also suggest that the move represented more than simply changing uniforms.
"If I had stayed in Boston, would it have been the same? I don't know," Sale added. "It's hard to tell, but because of the trade, I've found someone and got into some places and did some things that really helped me be healthy again."
That distinction matters when assessing the deal. Sale's Boston tenure included a World Series championship and some dominance, but injuries dramatically limited his availability late in his Red Sox career. Boston traded him after he made only 20 starts in 2023.
Atlanta, meanwhile, has received the version of Sale that Boston hoped it could keep healthy. In 2026, he earned his 10th All-Star selection and continued adding to his impressive Braves resume.
The trade will inevitably remain a fascinating what-if for both fan bases, particularly as Sale and the Braves enter another postseason chase.
This article was originally published on Forbes.com

Xavier Edwards Still Out for Marlins


Keith Hernandez




Sep 25, 2026, 6:07 PM ET
Miami Marlins middle infielder Xavier Edwards (thumb) remains out of the starting nine for Friday's series opener at home against the division-rival Atlanta Braves, per MLB.com. Jared Serna will make another start at second base for the Fish and will hit in the nine-hole against Braves left-hander Ray Kerr. This will be Edwards' fifth straight missed game after he aggravated a left-thumb injury last Saturday against the San Diego Padres. The Marlins have not rushed the 27-year-old back after being eliminated from playoff contention. At this point, he only has two more chances to return before the end of the regular season on Saturday and Sunday against Atlanta. The switch-hitting middle infielder was having a second straight solid season for the Fish this year, slashing .280/.360/.371 with a .730 OPS, a career-high six home runs, 52 RBI, 21 stolen bases, and 61 runs scored across 142 games and 595 plate appearances. Chris Sale just did something that very few pitchers ever get to do. He reached 200 strikeouts for the ninth time in his career. This feat places him in a group so small it barely exists. According to MLB.com Braves, Sale is now the only left-handed pitcher in history to join his idol Randy Johnson with nine or more 200-strikeout seasons. Nolan Ryan, Roger Clemens, and Tom Seaver are the only ones with more. That is a list of names that defines the game itself.
A Historic Night at Truist Park
The moment happened on Wednesday night against the Reds. Sale needed just one more strikeout to hit the magic number. Sal Stewart watched a called strike to conclude his 97-pitch outing. The 3-2 pitch looked inside, but umpire Derek Thomas called it a strike. Sale finished with 10 strikeouts in the 3-2 walk-off win. The crowd erupted as "Hard Workin' Man" blared through the speakers. Every infielder surrounded the mound to cheer him on. It was a perfect end to a regular season that defied all logic.
Most pitchers fade by age 37. Sale is getting better. He finished the year with a 2.16 ERA, a number that shocks the baseball world. The only pitchers with a better mark were Jacob Misiorowski (1.86) and Cam Schlittler (1.94). Among Braves since 1920, only Greg Maddux, Reynaldo López, and Warren Spahn have posted a 2.16 ERA or lower over at least 25 starts. Sale joins Justin Verlander and Roger Clemens as the only pitchers since 1950 to post a 2.20 ERA or lower with 25-plus starts at age 37 or older. Clemens and Verlander had 185 strikeouts those years. Sale blew past that mark.
Why This Changes the Legacy
People thought 2024 would be his last ride. He entered the season thinking it was the end. Then he exited with his first career Cy Young Award. That is a massive turnaround after injuries limited him to 151 innings from 2021 to 2023. His first three seasons with Atlanta all featured improvement for him. "It's amazing what he's doing at this stage of his career," the sentiment goes around the league. He is not just surviving; he is dominating the best hitters in the game.
The NL Wild Card Series Game 1 begins for him on Tuesday. The aggression he showed on Wednesday will be the same he uses in the playoffs. He knows he might not pitch more than five innings, but he made every pitch count. Although Juan Brito hit a leadoff homer, Sale held the Reds scoreless for the remaining 5 2/3 innings. That resilience is what makes him a legend. He is not just a pitcher; he is a standard for how the game should be played.
History is not written by those who play safe. It is written by those who keep hitting the corner at 37 years old. Sale has done it nine times. He has joined the immortals. The Braves have a chance to win it all, and they have the best pitcher in the world to lead them.

Chris Sale, de Atlanta, se mete a un club histórico con 200 ponches
El zurdo alcanzó la marca por novena ocasión en su carrera; a los 37 años, el estelar de los Bravos cerró una temporada espectacular y ahora apunta a octubre
Chris Sale volvió a hacer historia. El zurdo de los Atlanta Braves alcanzó los 200 ponches en una temporada por novena ocasión en su carrera, una cifra que lo coloca junto a algunos de los nombres más importantes en la historia del pitcheo de las Grandes Ligas.
La marca llegó este miércoles 23 de septiembre, durante el triunfo de Atlanta por 3-2 sobre los Cincinnati Reds, en un encuentro que terminó en extrainnings. Sale ponchó a 10 bateadores en 5.2 entradas y consiguió el abanicado número 200 al retirar a Sal Stewart en la sexta entrada.
El detalle no es menor. Con esta actuación, Sale se convirtió en el lanzador con más temporadas de 200 ponches desde 2013, además de convertirse en apenas el segundo pitcher zurdo en la historia de MLB con nueve campañas de al menos 200 ponches, solamente detrás de Randy Johnson, quien lo hizo en 13 ocasiones.
UNA LISTA CON PUROS MONSTRUOS DEL MONTÍCULO
La lista histórica de temporadas con 200 o más ponches tiene a Nolan Ryan al frente con 15, seguido por Randy Johnson con 13, Roger Clemens con 12 y Tom Seaver con 10. Ahora Sale aparece inmediatamente detrás de ellos con nueve campañas.
Lo curioso es que Sale consiguió semejante cifra a los 37 años, cuando muchos lanzadores veteranos ya han reducido considerablemente su velocidad y capacidad para generar swings fallidos. El zurdo, en cambio, cerró la campaña regular con 200 ponches en 162.2 entradas, además de una efectividad de 2.16, 14 victorias y 9 derrotas.
Y todavía hay más. En su última apertura de la temporada, Sale volvió a mostrar que su brazo está lejos de pedir vacaciones. De sus 97 lanzamientos ante Cincinnati, 12 alcanzaron al menos las 99 millas por hora, mientras que Statcast registró una velocidad máxima de 99.9 mph.
La velocidad ha sido una de las historias más llamativas de Sale durante 2026. MLB ya había documentado que el zurdo estaba lanzando más fuerte que en buena parte de sus últimas temporadas, incluso llegando a 99.6 mph con su recta de cuatro costuras en una actuación contra los Dodgers.
Su temporada también tuvo otra actuación espectacular contra Los Ángeles: el 27 de agosto lanzó una blanqueada completa de nueve entradas, ponchó a 11 bateadores y permitió solamente dos imparables, una muestra del nivel que mantuvo durante la segunda mitad del calendario.
El resultado final fue una campaña en la que Sale terminó con 2.16 de efectividad, 200 ponches y un WHIP de 0.98, números que lo mantuvieron entre los brazos más dominantes de la Liga Nacional.
El logro de Sale llegó justo cuando Atlanta ya había asegurado su boleto a la postemporada y, posteriormente, conquistó el título de la División Este de la Liga Nacional, el séptimo de la franquicia en las últimas nueve temporadas.
Ahora viene la parte verdaderamente importante. Sale está proyectado para abrir el Juego 1 de la Serie de Comodines de la Liga Nacional, si Atlanta mantiene el tercer puesto de la siembra. La Serie de Comodines comenzará el 29 de septiembre y se disputará a tres juegos.
El escenario todavía puede cambiar porque Atlanta busca mejorar su posición en la tabla, pero el plan del cuerpo técnico ya está definido alrededor de su principal carta. Chris Sale será el encargado de ponerle la pelota al guante cuando los Bravos arranquen su camino hacia octubre.
UNA CARRERA QUE SIGUE AGREGANDO CAPÍTULOS
El nuevo registro se suma a una colección de números que ya hacen de Sale uno de los lanzadores más destacados de su generación. En 2025 se convirtió en el pitcher que más rápido alcanzó los 2,500 ponches en la historia de MLB, al conseguirlo en apenas 2,026 entradas, superando la marca que pertenecía precisamente a Randy Johnson.
Además, Sale ya posee un Premio Cy Young de la Liga Nacional, ganado en 2024, y múltiples selecciones al Juego de Estrellas. Su trayectoria también incluye pasos por White Sox y Red Sox antes de convertirse en una pieza fundamental de Atlanta.
Ahora, a los 37 años, el zurdo tiene otro número redondo en la vitrina: nueve temporadas con 200 ponches. Y mientras los libros de historia comienzan a hacerle espacio, Sale tiene una preocupación mucho más inmediata.
Octubre está a la vuelta de la esquina y el brazo izquierdo de los Bravos todavía tiene bastante veneno.

Jacob Misiorowski is scheduled to take the mound one more time for the Milwaukee Brewers in the 2026 Major League Baseball regular season. If he gets through it without a blowup, he'll make Brewers franchise history in the process.
Misiorowski is leading the league with an eye-popping 1.86 ERA in 169 1/3 innings of work. Right now, the record for ERA in a single season by a Brewers starter is 2.36, which was set by Mike Caldwell back in 1978. Frankly, it would be difficult for Misiorowski to drop down and not break Caldwell's record at this point on Sunday in the Brewers' season finale against the St. Louis Cardinals. To put it into perspective, if Misiorowski allowed 10 earned runs on Sunday and didn't record an out, his ERA would increase to 2.39.
The odds of that happening aren't zero, but they're as close as you can get to it as possible. Even in the off chance that Misiorowski struggles, the Brewers could simply take him out if things aren't looking good.
History Is Coming For Jacob Misiorowski
So, on Sunday, Caldwell's record is likely to fall and Milwaukee will have a new single-season ERA champion. He has put himself in a position that guys like Freddy Peralta, Corbin Burnes and Brandon Woodruff never were able to. That's special. Burnes won a Cy Young Award in Milwaukee and his season wasn't anywhere near what Misiorowski has been able to do in 2026.
The closest player to Misiorowski in baseball in general has been Cam Schlittler of the New York Yankees, who has a 1.94 ERA this season so far. The closest player to Misiorowski in the National League has been Chris Sale, who has a 2.16 ERA.
Last year, Misiorowski got the baseball world talking when he made his big league debut and flashed an elite fastball and made an All-Star Game sooner than everyone likely expected. This year, he has taken a massive leap and has been the most dominant pitcher in the league and has put together a season for the ages.
He got the ball on Opening Day for the Brewers this season and now the 24-year-old will bookend the campaign with history on the line. Sometimes, baseball can put together storybook situations you can't find elsewhere. This is yet another example. When the 2026 season began, there were questions about whether he could hold up for an entire season throwing as hard as he does. He has answered every question. Milwaukee is lucky to have him and if it is going to go on a deep run, the righty is going to be a significant reason why.

Chris Sale has had a historic season for the Atlanta Braves.
Atlanta Braves left-handed ace Chris Sale reached 200 strikeouts for the ninth time in his career on Wednesday night. MLB shared the accomplishment with a post on X. The 37-year-old veteran hit the mark in Atlanta’s 3-2, 10-inning walk-off win over the Cincinnati Reds at Truist Park.
The milestone places Sale in company he has chased his whole life. He now joins Randy Johnson as the only left-handers in MLB history with nine 200-strikeout seasons.
Sale needed just one strong night to get there in his final regular-season tune-up before the playoffs. He struck out 10 over 5 2⁄3 innings and surrendered only a lead-off home run to Juan Brito. He reached the mark in the sixth inning, catching Reds rookie Sal Stewart looking for punchout No. 200.
The outing capped a remarkable year. Sale finished the regular season with a 2.16 ERA, his lowest since 2018, to go with a 0.984 WHIP. He also had exactly 200 strikeouts across 162 2⁄3 innings and 27 starts. He had five double-digit strikeout games along the way.
His consistency stood out most. Sale made 17 starts with one walk or fewer and pulled off 24 straight starts allowing three runs or fewer, a franchise record. He was nearly unhittable every time he took the mound.
Acquired from the Boston Red Sox before the 2024 season, Sale won the National League Cy Young Award and swept the pitching triple crown in his first year in Atlanta. He will not win the award this year, but only because Milwaukee Brewers right-hander Jacob Misiorowski is having one of the best seasons ever by a pitcher.
Sale’s resurgence came after several seasons in Boston were derailed by injuries. He did miss time in 2025 due to a freak accident where he fractured his left rib cage.
Still, he has been the unquestioned ace of the Braves rotation since his arrival, which has mattered a ton given how many injuries the staff has dealt with.
Atlanta clinched the National League East on September 20, its seventh division title in nine years. The title came despite lowered preseason expectations with a new manager in Walt Weiss and their disappointing season in 2025.
At 93-65, the club has basically locked up the National League’s No. 3 seed and home-field advantage for a wild card series at Truist Park.
Sale is lined up to start the opener, likely Tuesday, in his first postseason appearance since 2021.

Jacob Misiorowski has spent much of 2026 making opposing hitters look like they would rather be anywhere else. Now, the Milwaukee Brewers ace has one more regular-season honor to add to his remarkable year.
MLB.com kept Misiorowski at No. 1 in its latest Starting Pitcher Power Rankings, giving the 24-year-old his seventh straight appearance atop the list. Cam Schlittler, Chris Sale and Yoshinobu Yamamoto followed him in the top four as the regular season reaches its final days.
Misiorowski has certainly made it difficult to argue with the ranking. Through 29 starts, he is 15-5 with a 1.86 ERA, a 0.80 WHIP and 247 strikeouts over 169.1 innings. He also leads qualified starters in opponent batting average at .180.
That strikeout total is especially interesting because Misiorowski has one more start to reach 250. If he gets there, he would become the fourth pitcher in the last six years to reach that mark, joining Spencer Strider, Gerrit Cole and Garrett Crochet.
Jacob Misiorowski has plenty of competition behind him
Schlittler has given the Brewers star a legitimate challenger. The Yankees rookie owns a 1.94 ERA, second among qualified starters, and has quickly become one of the biggest stories in the American League.
Sale has been just as impressive for the Atlanta Braves. The 37-year-old reached 200 strikeouts Wednesday for the ninth time in his career, moving past Steve Carlton for the second-most 200-strikeout seasons by a left-hander. Only Randy Johnson has more.
Then there is Yamamoto, who jumped from No. 8 to No. 4. The Dodgers right-hander entered Wednesday with a 1.98 ERA over 10 starts since the All-Star break and a 0.87 WHIP for the season.
Still, Misiorowski remains the man everyone is chasing.
The Brewers right-hander has combined elite results with the kind of velocity that makes radar guns look slightly nervous. More importantly, he has maintained that dominance across an entire season.
Now he gets one final regular-season start before October.
At this point, Misiorowski has already made his case. The playoffs will simply give him another place to make hitters regret stepping into the box.

On Wednesday afternoon, the Blue Jays were eliminated from the playoff race. The team had a disappointing season.
Naturally, this raises the question: Is this the end for Max Scherzer?
We know he's likely to make one last start on Sunday in front of the Toronto Blue Jays' fans—even if it's on short rest.
That would allow him to have a fitting farewell start in front of his fans.
We imagine he'll be looking, in particular, to surpass Justin Verlander (who will throw a few pitches on Saturday) in strikeouts.
After his seven strikeouts on Wednesday, Scherzer is four behind his former teammate with the Tigers and the Mets.
But the question on everyone's mind is this: Will Scherzer seek to return to the majors in 2027?
For now, the pitcher is keeping everyone in suspense. He'll reveal his plans in the coming days, once the season is over.
Scherzer, who has 500 career starts under his belt, was the subject of an article (in The Athletic) on Wednesday morning stating that he is aiming for a 20th season in 2027.
It's unclear whether he'll achieve that goal, but that's what he's aiming for.
In reality, it will depend on whether he feels capable of pitching and whether a team he's interested in were to make him an offer.
It's still too early to tell if the stars will align… and if his body will hold up. After all, he's realized he can no longer pitch through injuries like he did when he was younger.
Personally, I get the feeling he wants to come back. He loves baseball too much, and I think he wants more than just to narrowly surpass Justin Verlander in career strikeouts.
And above all: I also think he doesn't want to be inducted into Cooperstown at the same time as Verlander, who's retiring on Saturday. We talked about it on the podcast last night…

El lanzador de los Atlanta Braves alcanzó una cifra histórica y reafirmó su dominio desde la lomita a sus 37 años
Chris Sale volvió a colocar su nombre entre los grandes lanzadores de las Grandes Ligas. El zurdo de los Atlanta Braves alcanzó la cifra de 200 ponches en una temporada por novena ocasión en su carrera, un registro que lo coloca dentro de un grupo exclusivo en la historia reciente de MLB.
El serpentinero consiguió la marca al ponchar a 10 bateadores durante la victoria de este miércoles 23 de septiembre por walk-off de los Bravos por 3-2 ante los Cincinnati Reds en el Truist Parkla y reafirmó una de las características que han definido su trayectoria: su capacidad para dominar a los bateadores mediante la potencia de su recta, su slider y una mecánica que durante años lo convirtió en uno de los lanzadores más difíciles de enfrentar.
Además, Sale se unió a Randy Johnson como los únicos lanzadores zurdos en la historia de MLB con nueve o más campañas superando los 200 ponches. La lista de pitchers con más temporadas de este tipo está encabezada por Nolan Ryan, con 15, seguido por Randy Johnson, con 13, Roger Clemens, con 12, y Tom Seaver, con 10.
Además de su cifra de ponches, el veterano cerró la temporada regular con una efectividad de 2.16, uno de los mejores registros entre los lanzadores calificados de MLB. Solamente Jacob Misiorowski (1.86) y Cam Schlittler (1.94) presentan mejores números entre quienes cumplen con los requisitos estadísticos.
Su campaña también lo coloca dentro de la historia de los Braves. Desde 1920, únicamente Greg Maddux —con efectividades de 1.56 en 1994 y 1.63 en 1995—, Reynaldo López —1.99 en 2024— y Warren Spahn —2.10 en 1953— habían registrado una efectividad de 2.16 o menor en al menos 25 aperturas durante una temporada con la franquicia.
MÁS INFORMACIÓN: Pete Alonso busca una marca histórica que nadie ha conseguido en 106 años de Grandes Ligas
Chris Sale vuelve a alcanzar una cifra histórica
La temporada con 200 ponches representa un nuevo capítulo en la carrera de Sale, quien alcanzó esta cifra por primera vez en 2012, cuando todavía pertenecía a los Chicago White Sox.
Desde entonces, el lanzador mantuvo una notable regularidad como especialista en ponchar rivales. Sus registros le permitieron superar nuevamente la barrera de los 200 abanicados en múltiples campañas con los White Sox, Boston Red Sox y ahora Atlanta Braves.
La marca confirma la trayectoria de un pitcher que ha enfrentado diferentes etapas dentro de MLB, incluidos periodos marcados por lesiones, pero que logró mantenerse como una referencia cuando estuvo disponible sobre la lomita.
Un dominio que se mantiene con el paso de los años
Chris Sale ha construido su reputación sobre su capacidad para generar swings fallidos y limitar la producción ofensiva de sus rivales. A lo largo de su carrera se ha caracterizado por mantener altos niveles de ponches y una presencia constante entre los lanzadores más destacados de la liga.

El zurdo explicó la importancia de mantenerse enfocado durante una temporada larga y destacó el trabajo colectivo detrás de sus resultados. “No lo haces solo. Es un esfuerzo de todos los días, de preparación, de trabajo y de tener la confianza de tus compañeros”, señaló Sale sobre el camino que lo llevó nuevamente a alcanzar una cifra histórica.
Su consistencia también le permitió sumar reconocimientos individuales, como el Premio Cy Young de la Liga Nacional en 2024, además de múltiples apariciones en el Juego de Estrellas.
Sale mantiene la potencia de su brazo rumbo a los playoffs
Más allá de los números, Sale demostró que su velocidad y capacidad de dominio siguen vigentes. En su última apertura de temporada regular, su recta de cuatro costuras alcanzó un promedio de 97.8 millas por hora, una de sus mejores marcas con ese lanzamiento como abridor desde 2018. ATLANTA - Chris Sale ha completado una de las temporadas más impresionantes en la historia de los Bravos. Pero, para él, la única temporada que importa es la que le espera a él y a sus compañeros de equipo.
Sale parecía un hombre con una misión clara: logró 10 ponches y aseguró otra temporada de al menos 200 ponches durante la victoria por walk-off de los Bravos por 3-2 ante los Rojos en el Truist Park. El lanzador zurdo afrontó esta última apertura de la temporada regular con la misma agresividad que mostrará cuando llegue la postemporada la próxima semana.
Dado que Sale está programado para abrir el primer juego de la Serie de Comodines de la Liga Nacional contra los Padres el martes, llegó a este encuentro sabiendo que tal vez no lanzaría más de cinco entradas. Afortunadamente, dispuso de un poco más de tiempo al terminar el quinto episodio con 199 ponches en su cuenta.
Tras retirar al dominicano Elly De La Cruz con un elevado al inicio de la sexta entrada, Sale concluyó su labor de 97 lanzamientos ponchando a Sal Stewart, quien se quedó mirando el tercer strike cantado. El lanzamiento en cuenta de 3-2 parecía estar ligeramente hacia adentro, pero la decisión del árbitro principal, Derek Thomas, permitió que los Bravos y sus aficionados disfrutaran de un momento especial.
Aliviado por no tener que retirar a Sale antes de que alcanzara la cifra de 200 ponches, el manager de los Bravos, Walt Weiss, caminó hacia el montículo para relevarlo. Los jugadores del cuadro interior rodearon el montículo y el veterano lanzador se retiró entre una gran ovación, mientras sonaba a todo volumen el tema "Hard Workin’ Man" del dúo Brooks & Dunn por el sistema de sonido del estadio.
Sale se une a su ídolo, Randy Johnson, como los únicos lanzadores zurdos en la historia de MLB que han registrado nueve o más temporadas con al menos 200 ponches. Nolan Ryan (15), Johnson (13), Roger Clemens (12) y Tom Seaver (10) son los únicos lanzadores con más de nueve temporadas de este tipo.
Sale permitió un jonrón inicial al dominicano Juan Brito, pero luego mantuvo a los Rojos sin anotar carreras durante el resto de su actuación de cinco entradas y dos tercios. El zurdo de 37 años terminó la temporada regular con una efectividad de 2.16. Los únicos lanzadores de MLB que cumplen los requisitos y presentan mejores marcas son Jacob Misiorowski (1.86) y Cam Schlittler (1.94).
Greg Maddux (1.56 en 1994 y 1.63 en 1995), el dominicano Reynaldo López (1.99 en 2024) y Warren Spahn (2.10 en 1953) son los únicos otros lanzadores de los Bravos desde 1920 que han registrado una efectividad de 2.16 o inferior en al menos 25 aperturas durante una temporada.
Sale comenzó la temporada del 2024 pensando que sería la última de su carrera, y la terminó ganando el primer premio Cy Young de su trayectoria. Las lesiones lo habían limitado a 151 entradas lanzadas entre 2021 y 2023; sin embargo, ha seguido mejorando a lo largo de cada una de sus tres primeras temporadas con Atlanta.
¿Cuántos lanzadores han registrado una efectividad de 2.20 o menos en 25 o más aperturas a los 37 años de edad o más desde 1950? Sale se une a Justin Verlander (1.75 en 2022) y Roger Clemens (1.87 en 2005) como los únicos integrantes de este grupo. Tanto Clemens como Verlander acumularon 185 ponches durante esas temporadas.
Esta fue también apenas la 27ma ocasión en que un lanzador de 37 años o más registró 200 ponches en una temporada. Existe un denominador común entre muchos de los lanzadores más recientes que han logrado esta hazaña:
• Sale, 2026 Bravos
• Charlie Morton, 2022 Bravos
• Morton, 2021 Bravos
• R.A. Dickey, 2012 Mets
• John Smoltz, 2006 Bravos
Sin duda, la edad no ha mermado la potencia del brazo de Sale. Su recta de cuatro costuras promedió 97.8 mph durante su última apertura de la temporada regular. Esa cifra igualó el tercer promedio más alto que ha logrado con este lanzamiento en cualquier partido como abridor, una marca que había alcanzado por última vez en 2018. Realizó cuatro lanzamientos a 99.5 mph o más rápido.
"Es increíble lo que está haciendo en esta etapa de su carrera", comentó Weiss. "Diría que su velocidad es tan buena o mejor que en cualquier momento de su carrera como abridor, lo cual es asombroso. Dadas las lesiones que sufrió durante sus años en Boston y su regreso tras ellas, es realmente una maravilla. Sí, algo verdaderamente especial".

ATLANTA (AP) — Chris Sale struck out 10 and reached 200 Ks for the season, Mauricio Dubón delivered a winning RBI single in the 10th inning, and the Atlanta Braves defeated the Cincinnati Reds 3-2 on Wednesday night.
Matt Olson and Austin Riley hit solo homers for the Braves. Brent Suter (3-2) worked a scoreless 10th inning and earned the win.
Sale went 5 2/3 innings and was removed after recording his third strikeout of the game of Reds rookie Sal Stewart. The 37-year-old left-hander has reached 200 strikeouts nine times, which is the most of any pitcher since 2013. In his final start before the postseason, he allowed one run on four hits. Sale hit at least 99 mph on the radar gun on 12 of his 97 pitches.
Olson’s home run was his 41st of the season and tied the game at 1 in the sixth. Riley's homer tied the game at 2 in the seventh. Dubón was 2 for 4 with a walk and extended his hitting streak to 10 games.
Reds right fielder Juan Brito led off the game with a home run to center field off Sale. He went 2 for 4, including his third homer of the season.
Braves reliever Robert Suarez pitched for the first time since June 19 after being sidelined due to elbow inflammation. He pitched the seventh inning and gave up a leadoff triple to Matt McLain and a sacrifice fly to Will Banfield that gave the Reds a 2-1 lead. He threw 13 pitches.
Braves right fielder Ronald Acuña Jr. sat out after suffering a bone bruise when he fouled a ball off his shin in Tuesday's 4-0 loss to the Reds. Braves manager Walt Weiss said Acuña was asking to play and felt he could play right field Wednesday, but the Braves decided to be cautious with a postseason berth clinched.
Up next
Braves RHP Tyler Mahle (7-10, 3.81) will make his final start before the postseason against Reds RHP Brady Singer (6-15, 5.67) in the series finale Thursday.

In what will likely be his last regular season start for the Atlanta Braves this season, Chris Sale will be facing off against Andrew Abbott and the Cincinnati Reds.
Chris Sale is not the front runner for the Cy Young award, but will most certainly get some second and third place votes with his 2.18 ERA, 30.3 percent strikeout rate, and league leading strikeout to walk ratio of 6.13. Sale also leads the NL is best HR rate of 0.5 per nine innings, and best walk rate in the NL of 4.9 percent.
Side note, Chris Sale has the best career strikeout to walk ratio of all-time. Sale has also pitched 157.0 innings thus far this season, which is hurting his Cy Young chances to guys like Jacob Misiorowski. It could be argued that he has passed his fellow competitor Cristopher Sánchez, but Sánchez has a whopping 200.0 IP which is second in MLB behind Sandy Alcantara.
The Braves got a scare yesterday when Ronald Acuña fouled a ball off his shin, but luckily all the tests came back negative. The Braves have already clinched the division so a loss to the Reds yesterday was not a huge deal except the chances of a playoff bye are quickly fading. The offense looked bad again, so hopefully they can catch a spark again before the playoffs take off.
No Braves player has faced Abbott more than five at-bats. Ha-Seong Kim has a HR in his four at-bats and Ozzie Albies has a .600 average. Michael Harris has struggled to an OPS of .400 in his five at-bats, and Mauricio Dubón and Mike Yastrzemski are hitless in their three at-bats. Austin Riley is also hitless in five at-bats.
It is hard to make any type of prediction on such a limited history, but we can look at Abbott's numbers and see his 4.70 ERA is approximately eleven percent below average and his 1.472 WHIP is the worst of his four year career. This season he has struggled with walks giving up 4.2 per nine innings. The Braves need to be patient this even and take advantage of his weakness. It is no secret that the Braves struggle in the walk department. Their 7.7 percent is the third worst in MLB. To be fair, they strike out at a lower rate than the average team this season, but walks get runners on base to knock in.
The Reds are in the bottom six in RP ERA this season. The Braves have feasted on RPs all season long. The key to the game tonight seems to be be patient against Abbott because he gives up a lot of walks. Get to the bullpen, and strike. Chris Sale should keep the runs low to make this a pretty easy win on paper. The question is how many players will be resting today, especially with a high likelihood that Acuña will be letting his leg heal.

Sixteen MLB games are on the board for Wednesday, September 23, and Eric Lindquist is treating it like the calendar demands: light on volume, heavier on conviction. "Not a lot of volume, quite a few plays," he said early in the show, and with the playoffs bearing down and lines already moving overnight, he picked his spots across the full board rather than forcing something in every window. He came into the day up slightly after a Tuesday that leaned on a PrizePicks card headlined by Mickey Moniac's home run at plus-475, and he's carrying that same selectivity into Wednesday: seven official plays, a handful of leans he never turned into bets, and a lot of games he talked through and walked away from entirely.
Mike Trout — Lindy's one MLB home run swing on today's board.
The Quick Answer
Lindy's Wednesday, September 23 card has seven official plays: Mike Trout (LAA) to hit a home run against left-hander Jeffrey Springs at plus-350, Toronto's moneyline in the bullpen-game second half of their Baltimore doubleheader at minus-108, Philadelphia's moneyline against Milwaukee at plus-124, the under 7.5 total for Cardinals-Pirates at even money, the over 8.5 total for White Sox-Royals at minus-107, Foster Griffin (CLE) for 5-plus strikeouts against a watered-down Red Sox lineup, and the Dodgers' moneyline against San Francisco in a "coin-flippy" spot with Yamamoto on the mound. Beyond that card, he talked through moneyline leans on Houston and the Yankees that never became bets, and passed on several other games entirely. The full breakdown is below.

Seven plays spread across seven different games, and a common thread runs through them: none of them lean on chasing a hot lineup. They're built on pitching matchups, park and weather notes, and one hitter the market has priced wrong.
His Home Run Play: Mike Trout Against A Lefty Who Can't Miss Bats
Lindy called this "an interesting one" the moment he got to it, and he was upfront that his own history with Mike Trout hasn't been profitable. But the numbers here pulled him in anyway. Trout is running a .221 expected ISO against left-handed pitching this year against just a .157 realized mark, a gap Lindy pointed to directly as evidence he's been unlucky rather than declining. Trout also strikes out at a sub-20% clip against left-handers, which matters against Jeffrey Springs, a southpaw Lindy said has "given up crazy boatloads of power to lefties and righties alike" this season. The Angels don't have much protection behind Trout from the left side of the plate, either. Lindy singled out Zach Neto as the only other left-handed bat he trusts in that lineup, and even called his price short. Mike Trout (LAA) to hit a home run against Jeffrey Springs, priced at plus-350 when Lindy made the call and sitting at plus-326 as of this recording, his only home run swing on a board that was mostly barren for the long ball.
Toronto Moneyline: The Bullpen Game Angle
The Blue Jays and Orioles are playing a doubleheader to make up a Tuesday rainout, and Lindy split his read on the two games. In the opener, he weighed Max Scherzer against Chris Bassett and talked himself out of the Toronto side, calling it "much closer" than the market had it and passing entirely. The second game is where he landed: Toronto is running a true bullpen game behind reliever CJ Van, while Baltimore hands the ball to Trey Gibson with the clear goal of eating innings before the season ends. Both teams are out of contention and playing out the string, but Lindy still liked Toronto's moneyline in Game 2 at minus-108, noting it was surprising to see the price sit that close given the bullpen-game context.
Phillies Moneyline: Nola At Home, A Good Park For Lefty Power
Milwaukee sends Logan Henderson, a strikeout-heavy arm, into Philadelphia while the Brewers are trying to hold off the Dodgers for the top seed in the National League. Lindy's read is that Citizens Bank Park is exactly the wrong park for that matchup to play out cleanly, given how well it treats left-handed power, and he noted Aaron Nola has pitched much better at home over the past month with pronounced home-road splits in his favor. Philadelphia's moneyline at plus-124, sized at a half unit, smaller than his usual game-line play, but not one he skipped.
Cardinals-Pirates: Betting The Weather, Not The Names
This one came down to conditions more than personnel. Wind blowing in at 12-13 mph at PNC Park is, in Lindy's words, "very advantageous pitching weather," and he wasn't even certain who'd be on the mound behind the Pirates' starter given how unsettled that staff has looked. Matthew Liberatore gets the ball for St. Louis, and Lindy flagged that Liberatore's pitch counts in his last three outings (72, 69, 81) suggest he could be in line for regression at some point. Just not, in his view, on a cold, wind-in night at a pitcher's park. Under 7.5 at even money, his second play built around ballpark conditions on this card.
White Sox-Royals: A Total Built On A Shaky Chicago Arm
Lindy was blunt about this one, flatly calling White Sox right-hander Eric Fedde horrible, and he's not buying into him regardless of the platoon matchup. Seth Lugo gets the ball for a Kansas City club Lindy still expects to run out a competitive lineup. With both bullpens likely to see plenty of work behind shaky starting pitching, he landed on the total. Over 8.5 at minus-107, sized at 0.3 units, one of his smaller plays on the card, but one he called "an all right spot to dip your toes into."
Foster Griffin Strikeouts: A Lineup With Nothing Left To Play For
Cleveland still has real playoff stakes; Boston's season, in Lindy's words, is "completely done," with the Red Sox locked into their wild-card spot with nothing left to jockey for. That combination is why he's not expecting Boston's best everyday lineup on the field, and it's the setup behind his smallest play of the day. Foster Griffin (CLE) for 5-plus strikeouts, sized at just a quarter unit. Griffin's 14.5 outs-recorded prop got a look too; Lindy leaned the over but called the hold on that number too heavy to bet, so it stayed off the card.
Dodgers Moneyline: A Coin Flip With Ohtani Coming Back
Yoshinobu Yamamoto got bumped up to start Wednesday for Los Angeles after the Dodgers ran a bullpen game against San Francisco and Robbie Ray, and Lindy's read leans on two things: Los Angeles needs innings out of Yamamoto with no days off left in the schedule, and Shohei Ohtani is expected back atop the lineup after his bicep issue. The Dodgers are chasing Milwaukee for the top seed in the National League, which means a full night of scoreboard-watching alongside their own game. The price is "closer to coin-flippy," in Lindy's words, and he stopped short of a big stand, but he still landed on it. Los Angeles Dodgers moneyline against San Francisco, sized at a quarter unit.
Leans He Didn't Fire
Two more spots got real analysis without becoming plays, and the LEAN ≠ PLAY line matters here. Lindy called Houston's moneyline against Seattle "probably the closest play I've got here on a lean section" given George Kirby's fading strikeout stuff and Houston's clear edge in stakes, but he stopped short of actually betting it. The Yankees' moneyline against Tampa Bay at minus-157 got a similar treatment: Lindy reasoned that a watered-down Rays lineup the day after clinching the AL East justifies the price even with the extra juice, but he flagged the number as more than he'd normally pay, so it stays a lean rather than a confirmed play. A thinner look at Minnesota's moneyline against a struggling Giants lineup also never got a price attached or a firm commitment.
Games He Passed On Entirely
Several more games got attention and no play. A pitcher's matchup drawing a righty-heavy Washington lineup fronted by CJ Abrams got a look, but Lindy said he didn't need to force a bet on that game. The Reds-Braves game drew a lean toward the under on Chris Sale's inflated strikeout total, but Lindy said the whole game was "very tough to bet" and left it alone. The Atlanta Braves have clinched a spot in the playoffs, winning the National League East division this year.
But Atlanta is looking for a little more than just that as the postseason gets going next week. Atlanta is still in the running for a top-two seed in the NL, but they find themselves sitting four games back as the last week of the regular season gets going.
Atlanta is coming off a three-game sweep of the Houston Astros, giving themselves some confidence coming into the final week. But this team has some work to do to prepare for the playoffs.
The Braves will now be opening up a three-game series against the Cincinnati Reds this week, starting today. This will be the final home series for Atlanta during the regular season, and the team will be looking to stack some wins before the playoffs begin.
Atlanta has a chance to take advantage of playing the Reds, whose pitching has been poor this season. But the Braves will need to take care of business, while getting some help to avoid playing in the wild-card series next week.
Matt Olson Decision Announced by Braves
Ahead of the series opener with the Reds, the Braves have announced the lineup for the contest. Within the lineup, slugger Matt Olson will be hitting third for Atlanta, playing at first base.

Olson has been great for Atlanta this year, hitting .253 with 40 home runs and 89 RBIs, while posting an OPS of .830. His consistency in the lineup has allowed the Braves to be one of the stronger offenses in all of baseball.
Walt Weiss Leading the Charge For Braves
One reason for the Braves’ success this season has been the leadership from manager Walt Weiss. Atlanta has leaned on Weiss to navigate the long year, and it has resulted in a massive turnaround for this clubhouse.
“When I look back on it, it was too much,” Weiss said. “That’s a big part of this job is having good timing for those conversations, whether it’s individually or collectively with your group. Your timing has to be good, or the message isn’t going to hit the same.”
Multiple players have spoken highly of Weiss this year, and how he has navigated everything. Braves ace Chris Sale gave some high praise to the manager after the team clinched the NL East crown.
“(With Walt) it’s like coaching down a highway and not coaching down a hallway,” Sale said. “ He lets you get here, but it’s not a correction at every turn. If you’re getting corrected going down a hallway, it’s this, it’s that. But down the highway, you get a little bit more leniency.”
The Braves will continue to lean on Weiss’s leadership throughout the playoffs, hoping for another run at a World Series title. But for now, the focus will be on the Reds series, with the Braves trying to get hot entering the playoffs.

On Sunday, as MLB’s regular season reached its one-week warning, the two most spectacular players of 2026 strutted their stuff. In Cincinnati, Cubs center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong singled, doubled, and hit his 45th home run in a 9-1 trouncing of the Reds. (He also stole his 38th base, putting him on the precipice of joining the 40-40 club.) Hours later, at Camden Yards, Brewers ace Jacob Misiorowski held the Orioles to one hit and lowered his ERA to 1.86 as the Brewers blanked Baltimore 3-0 for their major-league-leading (and franchise-record) 98th win.
A season’s most sensational player isn’t always its most valuable player—see Cal Raleigh last year—but PCA and the Miz check both boxes. They lead the majors in FanGraphs WAR for hitters and pitchers, respectively, and will win the MVP and Cy Young awards in the National League (which has established itself as the stronger circuit by owning the American League 375–323 in interleague play). PCA and the Miz; the Miz and PCA: Already All-Stars in 2025, they’ve made large leaps this year. The Cub has bolstered his bat speed and drawn more walks; the Brewer has upped his pitch speed and issued fewer walks. Born nine days apart in the spring of 2002, the two 24-year-old terrors of the NL Central have set the standards for hitting and pitching excellence and, in the process, made themselves the player stories of the season. In an MLB campaign whose compressed standings have caused fans to wonder which teams, if any, are actually good (especially in the AL, where the .500 Rangers lead the AL West), the left-handed hitter and right-handed hurler—whose clubs may meet in October—have left little doubt about their own extreme skills.
There’s also little doubt about how those skills stack up against each other—or, at least, what those skills are worth when they’re applied on the field. The “WAR leader” label lumps PCA and Misiorowski together as peerless players. If we had to choose between them, though, the answer would be easy: The Miz wins most of their head-to-head battles, but PCA wins the WAR. Crow-Armstrong, who’s hit .280/.371/.578 with superlative defense in center, has been much more valuable than Misiorowski, who’s held hitters to a .159/.225/.250 line and who’s struck out 247 batters (including PCA six times) while walking only 42 (including PCA twice). That’s no surprise: It’s now the norm for baseball’s best hitter to be a good deal better, WAR-wise, than baseball’s best pitcher. Which, in turn, tells us a lot about how hitter and pitcher usage—and entertainment value—have evolved.
Take Sunday’s action. PCA played the whole game in center, even though the Cubs had built a comfortable lead by the halfway point. The Miz, meanwhile, exited after three innings and 44 pitches, with the Brew Crew clinging to a 1-0 lead. With home field advantage throughout October up for grabs, Milwaukee still had something to play for. But the Brewers elected to take it easy on their flamethrower, who has already exceeded his 2025 workload (including the playoffs) by 28 innings. As a result, Misiorowski amassed just 62 percent of the WAR PCA did on Sunday—and, on the whole, he’s managed only 63 percent of the WAR PCA has produced this season (6.5 vs. 10.4).
It wasn’t always the case that baseball’s best hitter would leave baseball’s best pitcher in his dust on the combined WAR leaderboard. The chart below compares the values of FanGraphs’ hitting and pitching WAR leaders for each season dating back to the beginning of the DH era in 1973. To smooth out year-to-year variation, each bar represents a five-year rolling average of the annual hitter-minus-pitcher WAR gaps from the listed season plus the four preceding seasons. Thus, the value for 1973 is really the average of the figures from 1969 to 1973, and the value for 2026 is really the average of the figures from 2022 to 2026.
At the dawn of the DH era, when the iron men of the mound were still routinely topping 300 innings, the best pitchers were worth more than the best hitters. Pitchers also reigned supreme around the turn of the century, when the likes of Roger Clemens, Kevin Brown, and Randy Johnson were still topping 250 dominant innings, and Pedro Martínez posted the best pitching season ever by fWAR in 1999 (in a then-paltry 213 1/3 innings, which would lead both leagues in 2026). All in all, from the beginning of the DH era through the end of the 20th century, the leading hitter in any given year was worth only about half a WAR more than the leading pitcher, on average. From 1970 through 2000, the best hitter out-WARed the best pitcher 18 times, while a pitcher took the top spot 13 times. The battle for the title of baseball’s best player was typically close to a toss-up between the most overpowering pitcher and the biggest bat.
Over the past quarter century, though, the hitters have won in a walk. Beginning with 2001, when Barry Bonds morphed into his BALCO-boosted final form, the leading hitter has been about two wins better, on average, than the leading pitcher, enough to declare a conclusive victor despite the metric’s margin of error. During that span, best hitters have led best pitchers 25 seasons to one, with only Corbin Burnes’s slim edge over Trea Turner in 2021 preventing a clean sweep. And the gap is growing: Over the past five years, the leading hitter has been a full four wins better, on average, than the leading pitcher. In other words, baseball’s best pitchers aren’t worth what they used to be—but its best batters are.
This isn’t just a function of the no. 1 hitter lapping the no. 1 pitcher; although the average leads are less pronounced, the same trend appears when we expand the pool to each year’s top five hitters and top five pitchers.
The wide disparity in recent seasons stems in part from an unusually strong run by baseball’s best hitters. The average of 10.4 WAR generated by the hitting WAR leaders in the past five years (Aaron Judge three times, and Ronald Acuña Jr. and PCA once each) is the highest total of any five-season stretch since Bonds, Alex Rodriguez, and Albert Pujols in the early-to-mid 2000s—and, before that, Mickey Mantle, Willie Mays, and Ernie Banks in the late 1950s and Babe Ruth, Jimmie Foxx, and Lou Gehrig in the early 1930s. But it’s also a product of the lowest-ever five-year average WAR tally for pitching pacers (6.4), with the exception of the pandemic-suppressed 2019 to 2023 period and a late-’50s stretch of historically lackluster leading arms.
The culprit isn’t much of a mystery: It’s the playing-time totals. Modern pitchers are working smarter, not harder. (Or, if we want to be charitable, similarly hard, but in shorter bursts.) Collectively, pitchers throw roughly the same number of innings as ever, and accrue just as much WAR. (FanGraphs allots 1,000 WAR leaguewide per season, with 57 percent going to hitters and 43 percent apportioned to pitchers.) But those innings and WAR are distributed across many more arms than they used to be, as innings eating nears extinction and the starting-pitcher protagonist of the past fades from view. This season will either match last year’s all-time full-season low of three 200-plus-inning pitchers, or further reduce the record, depending on whether Michael Wacha (who’s sitting at 194 1/3 frames) joins Sandy Alcantara and Cristopher Sánchez in the 200-inning club in his final start.
Modern major leaguers’ workload diminution is much more apparent for pitchers than hitters. The chart below shows the number of hitters and pitchers who qualified for the batting title and ERA title, respectively, in each season of MLB’s 30-team era (since 1998, excluding 2020). The height of the bars (blue for hitters, orange for pitchers) indicates the number of qualifying players; the numbers above each bar (which could still increase slightly for 2026) denote the average number of plate appearances or innings within each year’s qualifying cohort.
Matt Olson aside, hitters aren’t totally immune to load management. Relative to the late 1990s, the number of qualifying hitters per season has sunk by about 15 percent, and the average number of plate appearances among qualifying hitters has been trimmed by a couple percent. But that’s nothing compared to the cratering of pitcher playing time. The number of qualifying pitchers per season has plummeted by nearly 50 percent, and the average number of innings among the remaining qualifiers has dropped by upwards of 10 percent.
Hence the ho-hum WAR totals mustered of late by baseball’s best pitchers, in an era of familiarity-effect avoidance, rampant pitcher injuries and, relatedly, an increased emphasis on max-effort throwing. As dazzling as today’s top arms are on an inning-per-inning basis—especially fastball-slider monsters like Mason Miller, whose outings are mostly contained to one frame—their GIFable filth comes at a cost. They can’t have both blistering stuff and exceptional staying power.
There’s no perfect substitute for the bulk starters used to supply. In 2019, for instance, Astros starter Gerrit Cole broke J.R. Richard’s single-season franchise record for strikeouts, 40 years after Richard’s nasty 1979 campaign. That accomplishment led to a sentimental meeting on the mound between past and present Astros aces, less than two years before Richard’s death. But although Cole surpassed Richard’s strikeout total, he couldn’t match his complete contribution: Richard threw 80 more innings, and recorded 8.9 WAR to Cole’s 7.5. Even Cole’s 212 1/3 innings in 2019 would be a standout total today; beyond Burnes in 2021, no pitcher since Cole has broken the 7-WAR wall.
On a long enough timescale, almost everything in sports circles back around. Someday, new rules might restore the starter’s lost luster, or overdue expansion might lower the major league replacement level and make the most competent pitchers look like WARlords again. League-leading hitters of the 2020s may be mogging their pitching counterparts when we focus on the DH era, but if we go back to the beginning of the National League, when hurlers who threw 400, 500, or 600 innings ruled the roost, we spot two subsequent stretches when the best bats had it even better than they do now: that late-’50s, offense-friendly low ebb for aces, and the 1920s and early ’30s, when Babe Ruth reinvented offense and broke baseball’s value scale. Once upon a time (or two), this batter-pitcher imbalance wasn’t so strange.
For now, though, we seem to be stuck in a phase where the cream of the crop of pitchers pales in comparison to elite everyday dudes. The sinking ceiling of starting-pitcher value may have implications for how pitchers are paid and staffs are assembled (not to mention how prospects are hyped). Free-agent pitchers make as much money per win as free-agent hitters, but if teams start expecting fewer wins from star pitchers than they do from star hitters, even the scarcity of healthy ligaments might not keep pitcher contracts from shrinking (and dragging down overall player pay). From the fan perspective, though, the more relevant byproduct of this modern mismatch in the value of leading hitters and pitchers is a shift in how we experience and describe standout seasons.
Because hitter playing-time totals today are comparable to what they were a century ago, we can still celebrate league-leading hitters via counting stats alone. PCA, for example, has played in every Cubs game this season, and started all but one. (As of today, he’s the majors’ sole 700-plate-appearance man.) We can convey his greatness just by marveling at how many homers he’s hit and bases he’s swiped; “the first 40-40 center fielder” would sound spiffy. If we want to dig deeper, we could note that only Triple Crown contender Yordan Alvarez stands in the way of PCA becoming the first player ever to lead the majors in both batting and fielding value in a single season, which would be a two-way feat almost as mind-blowing as Shohei Ohtani’s pitching/hitting heroics. And if we want to cite WAR, well, that’s easy: With six Cubs games to go, PCA’s season already ranks among the 50 best batting years in big league history, and above every season in the past half century save for four by Bonds, two by Judge, and one by Bobby Witt Jr.
In 2026, pitchers tend not to throw enough pitches or innings to reach famous milestones in single games, single seasons, or careers, so the case for Miz amazement can’t be made by hailing his membership in exclusive, storied clubs. With one regular-season start remaining, the Miz hasn’t quite cracked the top 350 seasons by pitching WAR. (No pitcher has posted a double-digit-WAR season since the Big Unit in 2001.) The 300-strikeout club has been closed to new recruits since Cole and his teammate Justin Verlander went in together in 2019. As for old-school wins, he’s tied for second in the Senior Circuit with 15, not that anyone pays much attention to that column on the player page.
To appreciate the Miz, we must resort to rate stats and modest minimums. Among pitchers with at least 160 innings in a season, Misiorowski ranks 13th in park- and league-adjusted ERA, 12th in park- and league-adjusted FIP, third in WHIP and strikeout-minus-walk rate, and second in strikeout rate. He has the lowest opponent batting average and rate of hits allowed per nine innings, too, which would be more eye-popping if people still cared about batting average or if the league were hitting more than .244. Ultimately, the summation rests on the smallest of samples: a single pitch. At peak pitch speed, he’s the hardest-throwing starter on record (and in all likelihood, ever), and damn near the hardest-throwing pitcher, period.
In a sense, the Miz is just as impactful as PCA—he just hasn’t had as many chances to make an impact. PCA has paired his 702 trips to the plate (offensive chances, essentially) with 380 chances in center, for a grand total of 1,082 opportunities to determine the outcome of a plate appearance. Misiorowski has faced 646 batters, or 60 percent of PCA’s combined plate appearances plus defensive chances. If we look at things that way—i.e., by doing dubious addition—then the Miz has done well to accumulate 63 percent of PCA’s WAR.
Plus, in defense of Misiorowski and the constellation of starters who trail him by 1 WAR or less—AL Cy Young lock Cam Schlittler, Cristopher Sánchez, Chris Sale, Jesús Luzardo, and Dylan Cease—the tale of the 2026 WAR leader is as much about Crow-Armstrong vs. the field as it is pitchers vs. hitters. Only Ohtani and Witt sit between PCA and Misiorowski on FanGraphs’ WAR leaderboard, and both only barely lead the Miz. WAR is always subject to retroactive updates, but if none of the players clustered between 6.4 and 6.7 WAR—Ohtani, Misiorowski, Witt, and Alvarez—finishes strong, this could be the first unabridged season since 1950 (when teams played 154 games) in which MLB’s second-most-valuable player doesn’t touch 7 WAR. Fittingly, the AL’s MVP contenders are as underwhelming as the AL’s contending teams.
“Underwhelming” doesn’t describe Misiorowski. Of course, the quality that makes the Miz so awe-inspiring—he throws hard enough to remove a mortal’s arm from its socket—is also what makes him so anxiety-inducing. It’s not as if hitters can’t get hurt by running, throwing, or swinging hard—or even by standing somewhere in the vicinity of the on-deck circle, as Crow-Armstrong’s teammate Alex Bregman (whose WAR total since the All-Star break is exceeded only by PCA’s) painfully learned on Sunday. But they aren’t as prone to season-ending disaster as a matter of routine.
We delight in PCA’s uninhibited, prolific play, while we watch the Miz’s impressive but sparing appearances through splayed fingers. As Joe Posnanski pointed out in July, pitching might be the only assignment in sports where “simply doing your job is so scary and treacherous.” Not because an opposing player might flatten you, or because you might, say, stumble and get sliced by a skate blade, but because the fundamental motion endemic to your duty is hazardous to your health. Which helps explain why teams have sought to limit how often pitchers perform that motion, for all the good it’s done them. As it turns out, making that motion more dangerous but doing it less doesn’t make UCLs safer.
Misiorowski has survived the season with only minor, sporadic complaints: a hamstring cramp here, a dead arm there. To forestall more serious trouble, and to preserve their most prized pitcher for the postseason, the Brewers have handled him carefully. Since the All-Star Game (which he missed), he’s tied for 72nd in innings pitched, with two pitchers (Jack Perkins and Zebby Matthews) who have matching 4.94 ERAs over that span. But in October, when off days allow for compression of a pitching staff, an unrestrained Miz may emerge to shoulder more of Milwaukee’s workload and make overmatched opponents and concerned spectators alike quake like Ralph Wiggum. Over a season, or even a series, a position player such as PCA may amass more value. But in any given game, an ace can still slay.

item.content:encoded:
The Colorado Rockies are 57–99.
Purple Row After Dark: If the Rockies could steal one player
An absurd rule for absurd times: if the worst team in baseball could steal one player from a playoff club, who should the Rockies take?
One more loss will give them their fourth consecutive 100-loss season, and they are almost certainly going to finish with the worst record in baseball.
These are absurd times for the Rockies, so I have devised an appropriately absurd rule to help them out.
The team with the worst record in baseball gets to steal one player from a playoff team.
There are, naturally, some restrictions. We’re freezing the playoff field as it stood before games on Sunday, September 20. The player has to come from one of those 12 teams, cannot be a pending free agent, and you cannot take the player who leads his team in FanGraphs WAR. The Rockies also inherit the player’s existing contract.
No, one player is not suddenly turning the Rockies into a contender. But could one poached superstar at least keep this thing from becoming five consecutive 100-loss seasons?
Here’s the board:
| Team | Off limits: fWAR leader | Highest available fWAR | Other players worth considering |
| Rays | Junior Caminero (5.2) | Drew Rasmussen (4.7) | Jonathan Aranda (3) |
| Guardians | Parker Messick (4.6) | Steven Kwan (3.4) | Gavin Williams (3.4), Brayan Rocchio (3.3), José Ramírez (2.2) |
| Rangers | Ezequiel Duran (4.6) | Jacob deGrom (4.2) | Josh Jung (2.9), Wyatt Langford (2.8) |
| Yankees | Cam Schlittler (6.1) | Ben Rice (4) | Cody Bellinger (3.9), Aaron Judge (2) |
| Red Sox | Willson Contreras (4.1) | Payton Tolle (4) | Ceddanne Rafaela (3.9), Ranger Suárez (3.7) |
| White Sox | Miguel Vargas (5) | Chase Meidroth (4) | Tristan Peters (3.9), Sean Burke (3.1) |
| Brewers | Jacob Misiorowski (6.3) | Brice Turang (5.4) | Jackson Chourio (4), Jake Bauers (3.6) |
| Dodgers | Shohei Ohtani (6.7) | Yoshinobu Yamamoto (4.7) | Max Muncy (4.3), Andy Pages (3.9) |
| Braves | Chris Sale (5.7) | Michael Harris II (4) | Matt Olson (4), Drake Baldwin (3.1) |
| Cubs | Pete Crow-Armstrong (10.2) | Alex Bregman (5) | Dansby Swanson (3.6) |
| Padres | Fernando Tatis Jr. (5) | Jackson Merrill (4) | Ty France (3.8), Mason Miller (3.7) |
| Phillies | Cristopher Sánchez (5.8) | Jesús Luzardo (5.6) | Zack Wheeler (3.5), Bryce Harper (3.4) |
For me, the choice comes down to Brice Turang, Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Aaron Judge.
Turang is probably the sensible choice.
At 5.4 fWAR, he would easily lead the Rockies, giving them a legitimate top-end player while immediately solving second base for the foreseeable future. He’s 26, hitting .266/.367/.441 with an .808 OPS, and brings value on both sides of the ball with elite range, strong baserunning and a 95th-percentile walk rate.
It would be a very easy way to make the roster better.
But the Rockies really need starting pitching.
Enter Yoshinobu Yamamoto.
He’s 14–8 with a 2.51 ERA, 178 strikeouts and a 0.87 WHIP over 179 innings. His Statcast profile is just as impressive: 100th-percentile pitching run value, 99th-percentile fastball run value, 95th-percentile offspeed run value and a 91st-percentile xERA.
Pitchers are risky, and Yamamoto comes with a lot of money attached. But it’s hard to argue with either the profile or the results, and the addition of the Penner family makes absorbing that contract a lot easier to imagine.
Speaking of high-priced items...
Aaron Judge.
Judge being available is basically a loophole created by our own stupid rule. Injuries have limited him to just 285 plate appearances, which is why he sits at only 2 fWAR, but he’s still hitting .241/.360/.511 with 15 home runs.
And the underlying numbers are still very much Judge: a .396 xwOBA, .569 xSLG, 94.0 mph average exit velocity and a 57.5% hard-hit rate.
It is very hard to look at that and say, “No thanks.”
After all, Aaron Judge is the type of hitter that, if he were playing 81 games a year at Coors Field, I might take out a small loan for season tickets.
So who are you stealing?

item.content:encoded:
One well-timed hot streak from a star player can be all a team needs to go on a big run.
While many key contributors struggled in the first half of 2026, several have picked it up big time since the All-Star break, lifting their clubs to late-season success.
Here are 10 players -- five hitters and five pitchers -- who have turned things around in the second half.
All stats are through Saturday's games unless otherwise specified.
Hitters
Alex Bregman, Cubs
For as good as National League MVP Award favorite Pete Crow-Armstrong has been lately, it’s actually Bregman who entered Saturday leading all qualifying hitters with a 168 wRC+ in the second half. The third baseman has a .298/.376/.609 slash line since the All-Star break, with his 17 second-half homers tied for fourth most in MLB.
Batting just .241 with nine home runs and a .695 OPS prior to the break, Bregman hadn’t exactly been meeting expectations after signing a five-year, $175 million deal with the Cubs. Now, though, he is up to 5.1 FanGraphs WAR, his highest total since 2022 (5.4). He’s been a big reason the Cubs are currently on track to host an NL Wild Card Series at Wrigley Field, and he will be a key bat in the middle of Chicago’s lineup in the postseason.
Steven Kwan, Guardians
With this week’s series win over the White Sox, the Guardians have surged into first place in the AL Central, in large part thanks to their leadoff hitter’s resurgence. In addition to his strong defense in left field -- Kwan has won four straight AL Gold Gloves in left to begin his career -- Kwan has been on fire at the plate.
After a disappointing first-half slash line of .225/.332/.282, including a .188 batting average in May, Kwan ranks second among qualifiers with a .347 average and is tied with Yordan Alvarez for first with a .435 on-base percentage in the second half. He has been setting the table admirably for a Cleveland club not getting as much as usual from third baseman José Ramírez (94 wRC+) and could help the Guardians secure not only the division title but a key first-round bye.
Jackson Merrill, Padres
Merrill took a step back in 2025 after finishing second to the Pirates’ Paul Skenes in 2024 NL Rookie of the Year Award voting, and the Padres center fielder appeared headed for further regression based on early returns in 2026. Merrill’s OPS was below .600 in late May as San Diego scuffled offensively, and he took a .219/.278/.350 slash line into the break.
Since then, Merrill has been a major reason why the Padres have a 38-21 (.644) record in the second half, tied with the Brewers for the best in the NL. He’s hitting .312 with 16 home runs, 48 RBIs and a .944 OPS in 59 games in the second half while playing standout defense in center. Merrill’s ability to recapture his rookie form has given the Padres a fighting chance to host a Wild Card Series, and he’ll be a key middle-of-the-order bat for the club.
George Springer, Blue Jays
Springer improved his OPS by nearly 300 points from 2024 to 2025, slashing .309/.399/.560 and finishing seventh in AL MVP balloting as Toronto fell just short of a World Series title. But the veteran’s numbers fell off again early in 2026, especially after Springer returned from a stint on the injured list for a left big toe fracture. He hit just .218 with a .677 OPS before the All-Star break, a period of rest that seemed to help considerably.
Springer recorded multiple hits in five of his first nine second-half games, finishing July with an .878 OPS, before batting .321 with an .858 OPS in August. While he has slowed a bit in September, battling multiple injuries, he has clearly found his footing at the plate. It might not be enough to drag a Blue Jays team dealing with a host of pitching injuries and a down year from Vladimir Guerrero Jr. to the postseason, but Toronto -- three games out of an AL Wild Card spot -- still has a chance.
Fernando Tatis Jr., Padres
While Merrill’s turnaround has been integral to the Padres’ second-half surge, Tatis’ production out of the leadoff spot has perhaps been even more important. The three-time All-Star began the season by scorching the baseball into the ground, going 55 games before hitting his first home run of the year on May 30.
The second half brought on a true power surge for Tatis, who homered three times in his first four games after the All-Star break and is now up to 24 dingers on the season. Entering Saturday, his 167 wRC+ in the second half was second in MLB, behind only Bregman. Tatis has raised his season OPS to .819 and has given the Padres a dangerous option at leadoff down the stretch.
Pitchers
Brayan Bello, Red Sox
Bello has turned the page on a dismal start to the season. The right-hander, coming off a 3.35 ERA as a starter in 2025, had a 9.00 ERA in his first six starts of 2026 and was moved to a bulk-relief role. Still, Bello took a 6.06 ERA into the All-Star break as the Red Sox finally began to heat up, winning nine straight games to end the first half and extending the streak to a franchise record-tying 15.
Bello has continued to impress for Boston, earning the start on Saturday and baffling the Rays over eight innings of one-run ball with 11 strikeouts. In the midst of a statistically unprecedented season, he’s found something that works, which has been crucial for a Red Sox team that has surged into postseason position and appears headed for another clash with the Yankees in the AL Wild Card Series.
Robert Gasser, Brewers
Tommy John surgery in June 2024 cut short Gasser’s promising rookie season, but he returned to make two solid starts at the tail end of 2025. The left-hander couldn’t sustain that success early in 2026, taking a 5.24 ERA into the All-Star break after being tagged for seven runs in three innings in his final first-half start.
Since then, Gasser has a 3.00 ERA in 57 innings of work after holding the Orioles scoreless over seven excellent innings on Saturday in Baltimore. In his first four September outings, including two against the Cubs, he has allowed just four earned runs across 21 innings pitched. With Brandon Woodruff’s 2026 return questionable and Kyle Harrison struggling mightily, Gasser’s improvement has made him an important arm for a Milwaukee team fighting to secure the NL’s No. 1 seed.
Tyler Mahle, Braves
Mahle owned a 5.13 ERA through his first 18 starts of 2026 for the Giants, but the Braves saw something in the veteran right-hander. Atlanta acquired Mahle ahead of the Trade Deadline for righty reliever Anthony Molina in a move that has paid considerable dividends for the Braves’ battered rotation.
Mahle has allowed only seven earned runs in eight starts for Atlanta, completing six or more innings in all but one of those outings. His 1.28 ERA in that span is the third best among all pitchers (min. 40 innings), and he’s been an excellent complement to ace lefty Chris Sale atop the Braves rotation. With Spencer Strider, Spencer Schwellenbach, Bryce Elder, Reynaldo López and Hurston Waldrep all on the injured list, Mahle has not only covered important innings but has been remarkably effective.
Aaron Nola, Phillies
Nola had an ERA above 6 in an injury-marred 2025 season, and his 2026 looked to be more of the same. The usually dependable right-hander gave up 20 home runs in the first half alone, tied for the fifth most in MLB, and headed into the All-Star break with a 5.75 ERA.
Since then, Nola has returned to near-vintage form for the Phillies, who have also gotten strong second halves from lefty Jesús Luzardo (currently on the injured list with left shoulder inflammation) and rookie righty Andrew Painter. After Thursday’s excellent start against the Mets, Nola has a 2.78 ERA in the second half, striking out 67 in 71 1/3 innings despite giving up 14 more home runs in just 12 starts. If he can limit the long balls, he could be at least an adequate replacement for Luzardo if the southpaw cannot return for the start of the postseason.
Brandon Pfaadt, D-backs
Pfaadt hasn’t quite lived up to his billing as a former top prospect just yet, but he’s shown flashes, such as his success against the Dodgers and Phillies during the D-backs’ 2023 World Series run. The righty's recent results have been quite encouraging, too: Pfaadt has a 3.01 ERA in the second half, including a run of 27 2/3 scoreless innings across four starts from July 28-Aug. 14. 
Optioned to Triple-A Reno in June after a poor start to the year, Pfaadt now has the chance to help pitch the D-backs into the playoffs, which might be difficult in an NL Wild Card race featuring the Cubs, Phillies and Padres. Pfaadt is lined up to start during Arizona’s final series of the season, a pivotal three-game set in San Diego from Sept. 25-27, and his outing could determine the D-backs’ postseason fate.
